title: Learning Multi-Objective Rewards and User Utility Function in Contextual Bandits for Personalized Ranking
abstract: Uses contextual bandits to learn multiple ranking objectives together with user-specific utility weights. It is transfer evidence for adaptive multi-objective personalization, but its utility optimization does not independently distinguish mandatory workplace obligations from soft preferences.

admission.reason: The abstract shows adaptive multi-objective personalized ranking, but all objectives enter a learned utility function; it does not establish the gap-2 distinction between non-negotiable response obligations or explicit user rules and softer preferences. The verified constrained-ranking candidate 2202.07088 is materially closer to the required hard-versus-soft separation, so this UNCHECKED paper does not justify an additional reading slot.

title: Conflicting information integration for decision support
abstract: Examines methods for integrating conflicting information from multiple sources for decision-support purposes and proposes an information-theoretic treatment. It is mechanism-level evidence for handling disputed multi-source state rather than an experiment on workplace briefing presentation.

admission.reason: The abstract concerns integration of conflicting information inside a decision-support mechanism. Gap-7 requires evidence about how stale, uncertain, disputed, or incomplete state is presented to users and how presentation affects decisions. This paper's described capability stops before that presentation question, and the uncertainty-visualization candidate addresses it experimentally.

title: Requests and Commitments in Email are More Complex Than You Think: Eight Reasons to be Cautious
abstract: Analyzes difficult cases in identifying requests and commitments in workplace email and documents several sources of ambiguity. It offers annotation and modeling guidance for obligation-oriented email processing.

admission.reason: The paper is relevant to obligation extraction because it catalogs ambiguity in requests and commitments, but this round has a more decision-relevant direct candidate on reliable annotation of requests-for-action and commitments-to-act. Reading both would largely duplicate the obligation-identification subproblem without addressing the missing interaction between obligations and personalized soft priority in gap-2. Identity is also UNCHECKED.

title: The Nature of Requests and Commitments in Email Messages
abstract: Develops precise utterance-level definitions for requests and commitments in workplace email and applies them to Enron messages. The work is directly relevant to distinguishing responsibility-bearing requests and promises from generic importance or likely user actions.

admission.reason: Precise definitions of requests and commitments are relevant, but the abstract primarily contributes the label definitions themselves. For the current gap, the 2007 candidate on whether these obligation-bearing acts can be identified reliably supplies stronger empirical evidence that obligation is a distinct annotation target. Reading both would spend a slot on substantially overlapping evidence without testing obligation-versus-preference prioritization. Identity is UNCHECKED.

title: Smart To-Do: Automatic Generation of To-Do Items from Emails
abstract: Introduces automatic generation of concise to-do items from emails in which a sender has committed to an action. The task provides a mechanism for turning commitment-bearing email content into explicit work items, although it does not evaluate longitudinal work-item state transitions.

admission.reason: The paper converts commitment-bearing emails into concise to-do items, but the target research problem begins after such work items have been identified: it needs longitudinal selection, persistence, state transitions, and priority across cycles and sources. The abstract does not show those capabilities, so the paper is adjacent rather than a material strengthening of the authorized streams for this round.

title: Adaptive User Modeling with Long and Short-Term Preferences for Personalized Recommendation
abstract: Models both long-term and short-term user preferences and adaptively combines them using time- and content-aware mechanisms. It is transfer evidence for personalization that changes with user behavior rather than remaining a fixed profile.

admission.reason: Long/short-term preference combination is relevant to adaptive personalization, but the abstract does not explicitly evaluate preference drift or adaptation after a user's interests change. The drift-detection recommender candidate addresses the open gap more directly, so this UNCHECKED paper is not admitted merely for general temporal personalization vocabulary.

title: Beyond SumBasic: Task-focused summarization with sentence simplification and lexical expansion
abstract: Develops task-focused multi-document summarization intended to answer a specified information need, combining content selection with sentence simplification and lexical expansion. It supplies foundational transfer evidence for requirement-directed briefing selection but has no longitudinal accepted-view state.

admission.reason: The abstract supports task-focused multi-document summarization, but it lacks longitudinal accepted-view state, novelty relative to previous briefings, persistent open items, or state transitions. The relevance/coverage/novelty candidate provides a closer transfer mechanism for the current omission-and-repetition problem, so this foundational but static paper would not materially strengthen the round.

title: Timeline Generation through Evolutionary Trans-Temporal Summarization
abstract: Generates timelines from time-stamped document collections using summaries that are related across dates. The method models temporal evolution and cross-date content selection, but does not explicitly represent persistent open, resolved, revoked, or superseded work-item states.

admission.reason: Trans-temporal timeline generation is relevant to evolutionary summarization, but the abstract does not model persistent actionable state or the new-versus-unchanged-open distinction. The Agent Newsroom candidate covers evolving chronological reporting while also explicitly addressing coverage, diversity, and redundancy, making this UNCHECKED paper comparatively redundant for the present gaps.

title: QMSum: A New Benchmark for Query-based Multi-domain Meeting Summarization
abstract: Introduces query-based summarization of long meetings, including queries concerning decisions and tasks, and evaluates locate-then-summarize approaches. It is relevant to decision- and action-focused content selection but does not by itself establish cross-conversation incremental work-item tracking.

admission.reason: QMSum is strong evidence for query-based long-meeting summarization and retrieval of decision/task-relevant spans, but the current high-priority gaps concern repeated-cycle state, cross-thread work-item identity, adaptive priority, and omission/repetition over time. The abstract does not address those missing capabilities, so its VERIFIED identity does not by itself justify a reading slot in this targeted round.

title: Influence of the physical effort of reminder-setting on strategic offloading of delayed intentions
abstract: Uses preregistered experiments to test how the physical cost of setting reminders affects strategic offloading of delayed intentions, including interactions with memory demands. It contributes evidence about the cost-benefit determinants of whether an outstanding intention is externally supported.

admission.reason: The study concerns the physical effort cost of setting reminders and strategic offloading. That is legitimate prospective-memory evidence, but it is peripheral to gap-5's needed signals for selecting briefing content based on forgetting risk, importance, urgency, recency, and personalized priority. Other reminder candidates address forgetting confidence, delay, and cue visibility more directly.

title: Lexicographically-ordered constraint satisfaction problems
abstract: Formalizes constraint problems in which feasibility constraints and preferences are represented separately and preferences can be ordered lexicographically. It supplies a transferable formal mechanism for obligation-before-preference decision rules.

admission.reason: The formal separation of feasibility constraints and lexicographically ordered preferences is conceptually compatible with obligation-before-preference rules, but the abstract is a generic constraint-satisfaction formalism rather than evidence about content selection, ranking, workplace obligations, or briefing outcomes. The VERIFIED constrained-ranking paper provides a substantially closer mechanism for T07, so this UNCHECKED candidate would be redundant and overly indirect.
